lessons.title: Binomial models and event probabilities
lessons.summary: Justify a binomial model and translate exact counts, tails and intervals into probabilities.
lessons.objective: Justify a binomial model and translate exact counts, tails and intervals into probabilities.
lessons.before: Use exact probabilities, combinations and conditional sample spaces from chapters 4–6. Short checks ask for exact fractions unless stated otherwise; follow each written question’s own rounding instruction. \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) counts trials up to and including the first success, starting at 1.
lessons.ideas:
A fixed number of trials and a fixed definition of success

For a binomial model, count successes in a fixed number n of independent trials. Each trial must have the same success probability p and only success or failure relative to the chosen definition. A trial may have several physical outcomes, provided they are grouped consistently into these two categories.

\[X\sim\mathrm B(n,p).\]

One count can be reached in several orders

For exactly r successes, one specified order has probability \(p^r(1-p)^{n-r}\). Choose the r successful positions to account for all orders.

\[\mathrm P(X=r)=\binom nr p^r(1-p)^{n-r}.\]

The support is the integers from 0 to n. The combination factor is not needed for a single specified order, such as failure on every trial except the last.

Translate the endpoint words first

At most k means X≤k; fewer than k means X≤k−1. At least k means X≥k; more than k means X≥k+1. A strict interval L<X<U includes only the integers L+1 through U−1.

\[\mathrm P(X\ge k)=1-\mathrm P(X\le k-1).\]

For at least one success, subtract the probability of no successes. For a small central interval, add its point probabilities. Do not use a complement with the wrong endpoint.

State the assumptions in context

Sampling a changing finite population without replacement is not exactly binomial. A common batch quality can also make outcomes dependent. Independence is a model assumption that needs a reason, not a consequence of observing repeated trials.
lessons.method:
1. Define success and what the random variable counts.
  2. Check independence, constant probability and whether the trial count is fixed or stops at an event.
  3. Translate words into an exact integer event before choosing a formula or complement.
  4. For conditional or staged models, identify the reached branch and denominator.
  5. Keep exact values until the final step; test neighbouring integers for a minimum or maximum.
  6. Check every feasible parameter branch and explain any stopping rule.
mistakes: Include the combination factor for an unspecified set of success positions.
At least k is complemented by at most k−1.
Do not interchange successes and failures without changing p.
A fixed number of trials differs from stopping on first success.

examples.title: A count model and its lower tail
examples.question: A sensor is tested 4 times independently. Each test fails with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). X counts failed tests. Give n and p in its binomial model, then \(\mathrm P(X=1)\) and \(\mathrm P(X\le 2)\).
examples.solution:
Failure is the defined success for this count. The trials are fixed, independent and share a constant probability.

\[X\sim\mathrm B(4,\frac{2}{5}).\]\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(X=1)&=\binom{4}{1}\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^{1}\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^{3},\\{}\mathrm P(X\le 2)&=\frac{513}{625}.\end{aligned}\]

Count table

\(x\)\(\mathrm P(X=x)\)
\(0\)\(\frac{81}{625}\)
\(1\)\(\frac{216}{625}\)
\(2\)\(\frac{216}{625}\)
\(3\)\(\frac{96}{625}\)
\(4\)\(\frac{16}{625}\)

Complete answers

Trial count n: \(4\).

Failure probability p: \(\frac{2}{5}\).

Exact-count probability: \(\frac{216}{625}\).

At-most probability: \(\frac{513}{625}\).

examples.title: Define success before using moments
examples.question: On each independent run a device gives red with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\), amber with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\), and green otherwise. X counts red-or-amber results in 5 runs. Find its success probability, mean, variance and \(\mathrm P(X\ge 1)\).
examples.solution:
Red and amber are disjoint categories of the same run, so add their probabilities. Then use the binomial moments and complement the zero-count event.

\[\begin{aligned}p&=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4},\\{}\mathrm E(X)&=\frac{5}{2},\\{}\operatorname{Var}(X)&=\frac{5}{4},\\{}\mathrm P(X\ge1)&=1-\frac{1}{2}^{5}.\end{aligned}\]

Count table

\(x\)\(\mathrm P(X=x)\)
\(0\)\(\frac{1}{32}\)
\(1\)\(\frac{5}{32}\)
\(2\)\(\frac{5}{16}\)
\(3\)\(\frac{5}{16}\)
\(4\)\(\frac{5}{32}\)
\(5\)\(\frac{1}{32}\)

Complete answers

Red-or-amber probability: \(\frac{1}{2}\).

Mean: \(\frac{5}{2}\).

Variance: \(\frac{5}{4}\).

At-least-one probability: \(\frac{31}{32}\).

examples.title: A specified order differs from an unspecified count
examples.question: There are 5 independent trials, each with success probability \(\frac{1}{2}\). Find the probability of exactly one success anywhere, of the last trial being the only success, and of at least one success. Choose the correct explanation.
examples.solution:
There are n possible positions for an unspecified single success. The specified last-success history is one sequence only. At least one is the complement of all failures.

\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(X=1)&=5\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{4}\frac{1}{2},\\{}\mathrm P(\text{last only})&=\frac{1}{32},\\{}\mathrm P(X\ge1)&=\frac{31}{32}.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Exactly one success anywhere: \(\frac{5}{32}\).

Only the last trial succeeds: \(\frac{1}{32}\).

At least one success: \(\frac{31}{32}\).

Correct conclusion: An unspecified single success can occupy n positions; the specified last success cannot.

lessons.title: Parameters, moments and integer thresholds
lessons.summary: Recover binomial parameters and find exact integer bounds while retaining all feasible branches.
lessons.objective: Recover binomial parameters and find exact integer bounds while retaining all feasible branches.
lessons.before: Use exact probabilities, combinations and conditional sample spaces from chapters 4–6. Short checks ask for exact fractions unless stated otherwise; follow each written question’s own rounding instruction. \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) counts trials up to and including the first success, starting at 1.
lessons.ideas:
The mean and variance identify different quantities

\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm E(X)&=np,\\\operatorname{Var}(X)&=np(1-p).\end{aligned}\]

If a standard deviation is supplied, square it before using the variance equation. The mean is measured in counts and the variance in squared counts. For a non-degenerate model with positive mean, divide the variance by the mean to find \(1-p\), then recover n. Check 0<p<1 and that n is a positive integer.

\[p=1-\frac{v}{\mu},\qquad n=\frac{\mu}{p}.\]

Variance alone can leave two values of p

For known n, \(p(1-p)\) is unchanged when p is replaced by \(1-p\). Solve the quadratic, retain both valid values, and use any extra mean or context restriction only afterwards. Label the smaller and larger answers clearly.

A probability target gives a bound, not an automatic integer

For at least one success in n trials the probability is \(1-(1-p)^n\). This increases with n. A logarithmic estimate can locate the boundary, but the original strict or inclusive inequality decides which integer is valid.

Check the neighbouring trial counts

For a minimum, verify that the proposed integer satisfies the condition and the preceding integer does not. If the target equals a boundary probability, changing ≥ to > can increase the minimum by one. For a maximum survival condition, check the next integer instead. Do not round a logarithm to the nearest integer without checking.

Check the original model after solving

A numerical solution with n not an integer is not a binomial trial count. A negative variance, or variance greater than the mean in a non-degenerate binomial model, signals an invalid parameter set. The deterministic boundary cases p=0 and p=1 need separate interpretation.
lessons.method:
1. Define success and what the random variable counts.
  2. Check independence, constant probability and whether the trial count is fixed or stops at an event.
  3. Translate words into an exact integer event before choosing a formula or complement.
  4. For conditional or staged models, identify the reached branch and denominator.
  5. Keep exact values until the final step; test neighbouring integers for a minimum or maximum.
  6. Check every feasible parameter branch and explain any stopping rule.
mistakes: Square a given standard deviation before substituting for variance.
Do not discard p and \(1-p\) without an extra restriction.
n must be an integer, not a rounded estimate that changes the given model.
Strict and inclusive probability targets can have different integer answers.

examples.title: Recover trial count and success probability
examples.question: X is binomial with mean \(\frac{4}{3}\) and variance \(\frac{8}{9}\). Find n, p and \(\mathrm P(X=2)\).
examples.solution:
Divide the variance equation by the mean equation, then recover the trial count. Verify p lies in (0,1) and n is an integer.

\[\begin{aligned}1-p&=\frac{\frac{8}{9}}{\frac{4}{3}},\\{}p&=\frac{1}{3},\\{}n&=\frac{\frac{4}{3}}{\frac{1}{3}},\\{}\mathrm P(X=2)&=\frac{8}{27}.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Trial count n: \(4\).

Success probability p: \(\frac{1}{3}\).

Exact-count probability: \(\frac{8}{27}\).

examples.title: A known mean supplies p
examples.question: X is binomial with 3 trials and mean \(1\). Find p, \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\), and \(\mathrm P(X=1 \mid X\le 2)\).
examples.solution:
Use np equal to the given mean. The conditional point is allowed by the upper bound, so divide its probability by the inclusive lower tail.

\[\begin{aligned}p&=\frac{1}{3},\\{}\operatorname{Var}(X)&=\frac{2}{3},\\{}\mathrm P(X=1\mid X\le2)&=\frac{\frac{4}{9}}{\frac{26}{27}}.\end{aligned}\]

Count table

\(x\)\(\mathrm P(X=x)\)
\(0\)\(\frac{8}{27}\)
\(1\)\(\frac{4}{9}\)
\(2\)\(\frac{2}{9}\)
\(3\)\(\frac{1}{27}\)

Complete answers

Success probability p: \(\frac{1}{3}\).

Variance: \(\frac{2}{3}\).

Point probability given the upper bound: \(\frac{6}{13}\).

examples.title: Inclusive and strict targets can differ by one trial
examples.question: Independent trials have success probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). Find the minimum n for the probability of at least one success in n trials to be at least \(\frac{37}{64}\), and separately to be greater than this target. Give the at-least-one probability at the inclusive minimum.
examples.solution:
The relevant cumulative probability is \(1-(1-p)^n\). Check the original inequality at consecutive integers; equality is allowed only for the inclusive target.

\(n\)\(1-(1-p)^n\)
\(2\)\(\frac{7}{16}\)
\(3\)\(\frac{37}{64}\)
\(4\)\(\frac{175}{256}\)

Complete answers

Minimum for an inclusive target: \(3\).

Minimum for a strict target: \(4\).

Probability at the inclusive minimum: \(\frac{37}{64}\).

examples.title: Variance can determine two branches
examples.question: X is binomial with 6 trials and variance \(\frac{5}{6}\). Find both possible success probabilities, labelled smaller and larger, and the corresponding means in the same order.
examples.solution:
Rearrange \(np(1-p)\) equal to the given variance as a quadratic. Its valid roots are complementary. No extra information here selects one branch.

\[\begin{aligned}6p(1-p)&=\frac{5}{6},\\{}p_{\rm low}&=\frac{1}{6},\\{}p_{\rm high}&=\frac{5}{6}.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Smaller probability: \(\frac{1}{6}\).

Larger probability: \(\frac{5}{6}\).

Mean for the smaller probability: \(1\).

Mean for the larger probability: \(5\).

lessons.title: Conditional and multi-stage binomial models
lessons.summary: Combine groups and batches correctly, retain shared causes and condition on the actual count event.
lessons.objective: Combine groups and batches correctly, retain shared causes and condition on the actual count event.
lessons.before: Use exact probabilities, combinations and conditional sample spaces from chapters 4–6. Short checks ask for exact fractions unless stated otherwise; follow each written question’s own rounding instruction. \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) counts trials up to and including the first success, starting at 1.
lessons.ideas:
Groups with different probabilities need separate counts

If two independent groups have different success probabilities, their combined count is not generally binomial with an averaged p. To get one success overall, split into one from the first group and none from the second, or the reverse. Add disjoint cases and retain their labels for a posterior question.

A batch event can become a new Bernoulli success

First calculate q, the probability a batch meets its stated criterion. If batches are independent and identically generated, the number of qualifying batches in a fixed set is binomial with success probability q. It is q, not the probability of a single item, that belongs in the second model.

A shared hidden choice can create dependence

A machine chosen once for a batch affects every item in that batch. Trials may be independent conditional on the machine, yet dependent after its identity is hidden. Mix the full conditional count tables using the machine-choice weights. The binomial variance formula using an averaged p need not apply to that mixture.

Restrict and renormalise a count table

Let H be a count event with positive probability. Intersect the requested event with H and divide by \(\mathrm P(H)\). For conditional moments, retain only the permitted count values and renormalise their probabilities.

\[\mathrm P(X=r\mid H)=\frac{\mathrm P(\{X=r\}\cap H)}{\mathrm P(H)}.\]

Given at least one success, the zero-count outcome is removed. The conditional mean is not simply np. Keep the condition explicit in both probability and expectation notation.
lessons.method:
1. Define success and what the random variable counts.
  2. Check independence, constant probability and whether the trial count is fixed or stops at an event.
  3. Translate words into an exact integer event before choosing a formula or complement.
  4. For conditional or staged models, identify the reached branch and denominator.
  5. Keep exact values until the final step; test neighbouring integers for a minimum or maximum.
  6. Check every feasible parameter branch and explain any stopping rule.
mistakes: Averaging different group probabilities does not generally give the combined model.
Use the batch qualification probability in the outer binomial.
Conditional independence does not force unconditional independence.
Conditional expectations need a normalised conditional distribution.

examples.title: One success overall has two disjoint routes
examples.question: Group A has 2 trials with success probability \(\frac{1}{4}\); group B has 3 trials with probability \(\frac{1}{2}\). All trials are independent. Find the probabilities of no successes overall, exactly one overall, and that the unique success came from A given exactly one overall.
examples.solution:
For one overall, use the disjoint cases (one in A, none in B) and (none in A, one in B). Keep the first case as the posterior numerator.

\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(A_1\cap B_0)&=\frac{3}{64},\\{}\mathrm P(A_0\cap B_1)&=\frac{27}{128},\\{}\mathrm P(\text{one overall})&=\frac{33}{128},\\{}\mathrm P(A_1\mid\text{one overall})&=\frac{\frac{3}{64}}{\frac{33}{128}}.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

No successes overall: \(\frac{9}{128}\).

Exactly one success overall: \(\frac{33}{128}\).

Unique success from A given exactly one: \(\frac{2}{11}\).

examples.title: A common machine makes the trials dependent
examples.question: Choose machine A once with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\), otherwise B. Test two items using that same machine. Conditional on its identity, outcomes are independent with success probability \(\frac{1}{5}\) for A or \(\frac{3}{5}\) for B. X counts the two successes. Find the marginal success probability of one item, \(\mathrm P(X=2)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\), then choose the dependence statement.
examples.solution:
Weight the two conditional binomial tables by the initial machine-choice probabilities. Calculate the variance from this mixture. Compare the joint success probability with the square of the marginal probability.

\(x\)\(\mathrm P(X=x)\)
\(0\)\(\frac{44}{125}\)
\(1\)\(\frac{52}{125}\)
\(2\)\(\frac{29}{125}\)
\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(S_1)&=\frac{11}{25},\\{}\mathrm P(S_1\cap S_2)&=\frac{29}{125},\\{}[\mathrm P(S_1)]^2&=\frac{121}{625},\\{}\operatorname{Var}(X)&=\frac{356}{625}.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Marginal probability of one success: \(\frac{11}{25}\).

Probability both items succeed: \(\frac{29}{125}\).

Variance of the count: \(\frac{356}{625}\).

Correct conclusion: The shared hidden machine makes the outcomes dependent unconditionally.

examples.title: Qualifying batches form the outer count
examples.question: A batch contains 3 independent items, each successful with probability \(\frac{1}{3}\). It qualifies if at least 2 succeed. There are 2 independent such batches; K counts qualifying batches. Find the qualification probability q, \(\mathrm E(K)\), and \(\mathrm P(K=1)\).
examples.solution:
First evaluate the inner binomial upper tail. Each batch then supplies one independent success/failure indicator with probability q; use that in the outer binomial.

\[K\sim\mathrm B(2,\frac{7}{27}).\]\[\begin{aligned}q&=\frac{7}{27},\\{}\mathrm E(K)&=\frac{14}{27},\\{}\mathrm P(K=1)&=\frac{280}{729}.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Batch qualification probability: \(\frac{7}{27}\).

Expected qualifying batches: \(\frac{14}{27}\).

Exact qualifying-batch probability: \(\frac{280}{729}\).

examples.title: Condition on at least one success
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm B(3,\frac{1}{3})\). Let \(H=\{X\ge1\}\). Find \(\mathrm P(X=2 \mid H)\), \(\mathrm P(X\le 2 \mid H)\), and \(\mathrm E(X \mid H)\).
examples.solution:
Remove the zero-count outcome and divide every retained probability by \(\mathrm P(H)\). Both the lower tail and the mean use the renormalised table.

\(x\)\(\mathrm P(X=x\mid H)\)
\(1\)\(\frac{12}{19}\)
\(2\)\(\frac{6}{19}\)
\(3\)\(\frac{1}{19}\)
\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(H)&=\frac{19}{27},\\{}\mathrm E(X\mid H)&=\frac{1}{\frac{19}{27}}.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Point probability given at least one: \(\frac{6}{19}\).

Lower tail given at least one: \(\frac{18}{19}\).

Conditional mean: \(\frac{27}{19}\).

lessons.title: First success and geometric models
lessons.summary: Use the first-success convention, waiting-time tails, memorylessness and finite caps correctly.
lessons.objective: Use the first-success convention, waiting-time tails, memorylessness and finite caps correctly.
lessons.before: Use exact probabilities, combinations and conditional sample spaces from chapters 4–6. Short checks ask for exact fractions unless stated otherwise; follow each written question’s own rounding instruction. \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) counts trials up to and including the first success, starting at 1.
lessons.ideas:
Count trials including the first success

Repeat independent trials with a constant success probability p until the first success. For 0<p≤1, the trial count T has support 1,2,3,… and is written \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\). It counts the successful trial as well as the preceding failures.

\[\begin{aligned}T&\sim\operatorname{Geo}(p),\\\mathrm P(T=r)&=(1-p)^{r-1}p.\end{aligned}\]

Tail events describe runs of failures

\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(T>m)&=(1-p)^m,\\\mathrm P(T\le m)&=1-(1-p)^m.\end{aligned}\]

T>m means all first m trials failed. T≥m needs only the first m−1 failures. For an interval, subtract the relevant tails with these exact endpoints.

The expected wait and a restart

\[\mathrm E(T)=\frac1p.\]

After a known run of failures, the further wait still has the same geometric law, because the remaining independent trials are unchanged. The expected number of further trials is \(\frac1p\); the expected total trial count includes the failures already observed. State which of these the question asks for.

Recover p from the correct information

The ratio of consecutive positive point probabilities is \(1-p\). The reciprocal of a given mean is p. In either case check the probability range and use neighbouring integers for a strict or inclusive waiting-time target.

A capped wait is a different variable

If \(N=\min(T,c)\), then N=c includes success on c and failure on every one of the c trials. Hence \(\mathrm P(N=c)\) is the probability of reaching trial c, not just of succeeding on it. Build the finite table and calculate \(\mathrm E(N)\) from it; the unrestricted formula \(\frac1p\) is not \(\mathrm E(N)\).
lessons.method:
1. Define success and what the random variable counts.
  2. Check independence, constant probability and whether the trial count is fixed or stops at an event.
  3. Translate words into an exact integer event before choosing a formula or complement.
  4. For conditional or staged models, identify the reached branch and denominator.
  5. Keep exact values until the final step; test neighbouring integers for a minimum or maximum.
  6. Check every feasible parameter branch and explain any stopping rule.
mistakes: \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) starts at 1, not 0.
T≥m and T>m have different failure counts.
Expected further trials and expected total trials are different after known failures.
At a finite cap combine terminal success and failure outcomes.

examples.title: A point, a tail and a cumulative probability
examples.question: Independent trials have constant success probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). T is the first-success trial, including the successful trial. Find \(\mathrm P(T=3)\), \(\mathrm P(T>4)\), \(\mathrm P(T\le 4)\), and \(\mathrm E(T)\).
examples.solution:
The point event needs 2 failures followed by success. The tail needs all first 4 trials to fail. The cumulative probability is its complement.

\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(T=3)&=\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^{2}\frac{2}{5},\\{}\mathrm P(T>4)&=\frac{81}{625},\\{}\mathrm E(T)&=\frac{1}{\frac{2}{5}}.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

First success on the stated trial: \(\frac{18}{125}\).

First success after the stated trial: \(\frac{81}{625}\).

First success by the stated trial: \(\frac{544}{625}\).

Expected first-success trial: \(\frac{5}{2}\).

examples.title: The further wait restarts, but the total clock does not
examples.question: T is geometric with success probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). The first 2 trials have failed. Find \(\mathrm P(T>4 \mid T>2)\), \(\mathrm P(T=4 \mid T>2)\), the expected number of further trials, and the expected total trial count.
examples.solution:
Cancel the already observed failure factor from numerator and denominator. The remaining future trials keep the original success probability. The total clock adds the known failures to the further wait.

\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(T>4\mid T>2)&=\frac{\frac{81}{625}}{\frac{9}{25}},\\{}\mathrm E(T-2\mid T>2)&=\frac{5}{2},\\{}\mathrm E(T\mid T>2)&=\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Conditional probability of the later tail: \(\frac{9}{25}\).

Conditional point probability: \(\frac{6}{25}\).

Expected further trials: \(\frac{5}{2}\).

Expected total trial count: \(\frac{9}{2}\).

examples.title: A consecutive-probability ratio gives the failure probability
examples.question: T is the first-success trial count in independent trials with constant success probability p. The ratio \(\mathrm P(T=3)\)/\(\mathrm P(T=2)\) is \(\frac{3}{4}\). Find p, \(\mathrm E(T)\), the minimum n with \(\mathrm P(T\le n)\) at least \(\frac{37}{64}\), and the minimum n when the inequality is strict.
examples.solution:
The consecutive point-probability ratio is \(1-p\), so subtract it from one; the mean is \(\frac1p\).

The relevant cumulative probability is \(1-(1-p)^n\). Check the original inequality at consecutive integers; equality is allowed only for the inclusive target.

\(n\)\(1-(1-p)^n\)
\(2\)\(\frac{7}{16}\)
\(3\)\(\frac{37}{64}\)
\(4\)\(\frac{175}{256}\)

Complete answers

Success probability p: \(\frac{1}{4}\).

Expected first-success trial: \(4\).

Minimum for an inclusive target: \(3\).

Minimum for a strict target: \(4\).

examples.title: The last capped value combines success and failure
examples.question: Independent trials have success probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). T is the unrestricted first-success trial. Stop after at most 4 attempts and let \(N=\min(T,4)\). Find \(\mathrm P(N=4)\), \(\mathrm E(N)\), the probability of success by the cap, and \(\mathrm E(T)\).
examples.solution:
The last value combines success on trial c and no success in the allowed trials. Their sum is the chance of reaching trial c. Use the finite table for N; \(\frac1p\) belongs to the unrestricted T.

\(j\)\(\mathrm P(N=j)\)
\(1\)\(\frac{1}{4}\)
\(2\)\(\frac{3}{16}\)
\(3\)\(\frac{9}{64}\)
\(4\)\(\frac{27}{64}\)
\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm E(N)&=\frac{175}{64},\\{}\mathrm P(T\le 4)&=\frac{175}{256},\\{}\mathrm E(T)&=4.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Probability at the capped final value: \(\frac{27}{64}\).

Expected capped trial count: \(\frac{175}{64}\).

Success probability by the cap: \(\frac{175}{256}\).

Expected unrestricted trial count: \(4\).

lessons.title: Repeated successes and mixed stopping rules
lessons.summary: Count success positions and terminal histories without applying an unrequired named distribution.
lessons.objective: Count success positions and terminal histories without applying an unrequired named distribution.
lessons.before: Use exact probabilities, combinations and conditional sample spaces from chapters 4–6. Short checks ask for exact fractions unless stated otherwise; follow each written question’s own rounding instruction. \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) counts trials up to and including the first success, starting at 1.
lessons.ideas:
A second success fixes the final trial

For the second success on trial t, the first t−1 trials contain exactly one success and trial t succeeds. Use the earlier binomial count and multiply by the final success probability. This is a construction from familiar methods; no negative-binomial theorem is required.

\[\mathrm P(S_2=t)=\mathrm P(\mathrm B(t-1,p)=1)\,p.\]

By a trial and on a trial are different events

The second success by trial m is equivalent to at least two successes in the first m trials. The second success exactly on m excludes histories that had already reached two successes earlier. A specified first-success position can impose further restrictions on those earlier histories.

Independent waiting processes keep separate parameters

For two independent first-success processes, multiply their point probabilities for a specified pair of finish times. Sum disjoint pairs for events such as simultaneous finishes within a finite window. Given both finish in that window, divide by the probability of that condition.

Sampling without replacement changes the hazard

A first marked item in a finite bag has a changing success chance after each failure. Use the finite tree or marked-position subsets. The initial success proportion alone does not justify \(\operatorname{Geo}(p)\) or the mean \(\frac1p\).

Stop immediately when either condition is met

In a race to two successes or two failures, SS and FF end after two trials. Only SF and FS continue. On trial three every remaining path ends. List these terminal histories once, multiply their probabilities and check that the total is one. Never append a trial to an already stopped history.
lessons.method:
1. Define success and what the random variable counts.
  2. Check independence, constant probability and whether the trial count is fixed or stops at an event.
  3. Translate words into an exact integer event before choosing a formula or complement.
  4. For conditional or staged models, identify the reached branch and denominator.
  5. Keep exact values until the final step; test neighbouring integers for a minimum or maximum.
  6. Check every feasible parameter branch and explain any stopping rule.
mistakes: The final success needs its own probability factor.
Second success on t excludes an earlier second success.
A first success in a finite bag need not be geometric.
Do not count histories after a stopping condition has already occurred.

examples.title: Fix the final trial of the second success
examples.question: Independent trials have success probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). Let S₂ be the trial of the second success. Find \(\mathrm P(S₂=4)\), \(\mathrm P(S₂\le 5)\), and the probability the first success is on trial 1 and the second on trial 4.
examples.solution:
For the second success on t, use exactly one success among the first t−1 trials and success on trial t. For the joint event, the first and final trials succeed and every intervening trial fails.

\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(S_2=4)&=\frac{108}{625},\\{}\mathrm P(S_2\le 5)&=\frac{2072}{3125},\\{}\mathrm P(S_1=1,S_2=4)&=\frac{36}{625}.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Second success on the stated trial: \(\frac{108}{625}\).

Second success by the stated trial: \(\frac{2072}{3125}\).

First on one and second on the stated trial: \(\frac{36}{625}\).

examples.title: Two waiting clocks can finish together
examples.question: Two independent processes have first-success trial counts T_A and T_B, with success probabilities \(\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\frac{1}{4}\). Find the probability both finish by 3, exactly one finishes by 3, and that they finish on the same trial given both finish by 3.
examples.solution:
For both, multiply the two cumulative probabilities. Exactly one has two disjoint routes. For simultaneous finishes within the window, sum products of matching point probabilities, then condition on both finishing.

\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(\text{both})&=\frac{259}{512},\\{}\mathrm P(\text{exactly one})&=\frac{113}{256},\\{}\mathrm P(\text{same within window})&=\frac{97}{512},\\{}\mathrm P(\text{same}\mid\text{both})&=\frac{\frac{97}{512}}{\frac{259}{512}}.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Both finish by the limit: \(\frac{259}{512}\).

Exactly one finishes by the limit: \(\frac{113}{256}\).

Same finish time given both finish by the limit: \(\frac{97}{259}\).

questions.prompt_html: Group A has 2 trials with success probability \(\frac{1}{2}\); group B has 2 trials with probability \(\frac{1}{3}\). All trials are independent. questions.title: Reading faults
questions.prompt_html:
A scanner reads 12 labels. Each reading has probability \(\frac{9}{50}\) of being incorrect, independently of all other readings. Let \(X\) be the number of incorrect readings.

  1. State the distribution of \(X\), giving its parameters.

    [1]

  2. Find the probability of exactly 2 incorrect readings.

    [2]

  3. Find the probability of at most 3 incorrect readings.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

There is a fixed number of independent readings with the same probability of error. Each reading is either correct or incorrect.

\[X\sim\mathrm B(12,\frac{9}{50}).\]

(b)

\[\mathrm P(X=2)=\binom{12}{2}\left(\frac{9}{50}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{41}{50}\right)^{10}=0.294\quad\text{(3 s.f.)}.\]

(c)

At most includes every count from zero to the stated bound.

\[\mathrm P(0\leq X\leq 3)=\sum_{r=0}^{3}\binom{12}{r}\left(\frac{9}{50}\right)^r\left(\frac{41}{50}\right)^{12-r}=0.845\quad\text{(3 s.f.)}.\]
questions.hint_html: Distinguish the probability of one reading from the distribution of the total number of incorrect readings.

marking_criteria.description_html: Correct binomial distribution and both parameters.
Uses the binomial probability, including the combination factor.
Identifies all counts from zero to the upper bound.

questions.title: Two acceptable classifications
questions.prompt_html:
A unit is classified as grade A, grade B or rejected. The probabilities of grades A and B are \(\frac{7}{25}\) and \(\frac{37}{100}\), respectively. Classifications of different units are independent. In a sample of 10 units, \(X\) counts those classified as either A or B.

  1. Find \(\mathrm E(X)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\).

    Give your answers in exact form.

    [3]

  2. Find the probability that at least 7 units have an acceptable grade.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The two grades are mutually exclusive for one unit, so add their probabilities.

\[p=\frac{7}{25}+\frac{37}{100}=\frac{13}{20},\quad X\sim\mathrm B(10,\frac{13}{20}).\]\[\mathrm E(X)=np=\frac{13}{2},\quad \operatorname{Var}(X)=np(1-p)=\frac{91}{40}.\]

(b)

\[\mathrm P(7\leq X\leq 10)=\sum_{r=7}^{10}\binom{10}{r}\left(\frac{13}{20}\right)^r\left(\frac{7}{20}\right)^{10-r}=0.514\quad\text{(3 s.f.)}.\]

questions.title: An unusually small or large count
questions.prompt_html:
On each of 9 independently selected days, a station uses its reserve pump with probability \(\frac{9}{25}\). Let \(X\) count the days on which the reserve pump is used.

  1. Find \(\mathrm P(X<2\text{ or }X>7)\).

    [3]

  2. Given that this event occurs, find the probability that the reserve pump was used on fewer than 2 days.

    [3]

  3. Explain why a binomial model may no longer be suitable if a single fault can affect several consecutive days.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(0.111\) (3 s.f.).

(b)

\(0.984\) (3 s.f.).

(c)

A shared fault can make the daily outcomes dependent.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The two events are disjoint. The permitted counts are \(0,1,8,9\).

\[\mathrm P(X<2\text{ or }X>7)=\mathrm P(X=0)+\mathrm P(X=1)+\mathrm P(X=8)+\mathrm P(X=9)=0.111.\]

(b)

\[\frac{\mathrm P(X<2)}{\mathrm P(X<2\text{ or }X>7)}=\frac{0.109}{0.111}=0.984.\]

The evaluation uses unrounded probabilities.

(c)

A common fault links the outcomes on different days. Independence can fail, even if the marginal probability for each day is unchanged.
questions.hint_html: Add disjoint tails first. For the conditional probability, divide by the probability of the entire condition.

marking_criteria.description_html: Uses the extreme-count event as the conditioning event.
Divides the lower-tail probability by the two-tail probability.
Links the shared fault to a failure of independence.

questions.title: Sampling from a restricted group
questions.prompt_html:
In a large archive, 35% of records are in format A, 25% in format B and 40% in format C. A sampler selects records independently from those in formats A or B only, with each eligible record equally likely to be selected. It selects 9 records.

    [3]

  3. Find the probability that both formats occur in the selected sample.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\mathrm P(A\mid A\cup B)=\frac{35}{60}=\frac{7}{12}.\]

\[\mathrm P(0\leq X\leq 4)=\sum_{r=0}^{4}\binom{9}{r}\left(\frac{7}{12}\right)^r\left(\frac{5}{12}\right)^{9-r}=0.302\quad\text{(3 s.f.)}.\]

(c)

Subtract the two disjoint events: all A, and all B.

\[1-\left(\frac{7}{12}\right)^{9}-\left(\frac{5}{12}\right)^{9}=0.992.\]

questions.prompt_html:
A company charges $180 for a service consisting of 14 independent checks. A check fails with probability \(\frac{2}{25}\). If more than 1 of the checks fail, the customer receives a single credit of $90; otherwise no credit is given. The company incurs a fixed cost of $65 for each service.

\[\mathrm E(\text{profit})=180-65-90\mathrm P(X>1)=87.10.\]

questions.title: Planning from an expected count
questions.prompt_html:
A calibration attempt succeeds with probability \(\frac{31}{50}\), independently of other attempts. A technician plans \(n\) attempts.

  1. Find the smallest value of \(n\) for which the expected number of successes is at least 8.

    [2]

  2. For this number of attempts, find the probability of at least 9 successes.

    [3]

  3. Explain why an expected count of at least 8 does not guarantee at least 8 successes.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(n_{\min}=13\).

(b)

\(0.410\) (3 s.f.).

(c)

Expectation is a long-run average; individual runs can fall below it.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\frac{31}{50}\) and \(q_0=1-p=\frac{19}{50}\).

\[np\geq 8,\quad n\geq\frac{8}{\frac{31}{50}}=12.903226.\]

Thus the smallest integer is 13.

(b)

\[\mathrm P(9\leq X\leq 13)=\sum_{r=9}^{13}\binom{13}{r}\left(\frac{31}{50}\right)^r\left(\frac{19}{50}\right)^{13-r}=0.410\quad\text{(3 s.f.)}.\]

(c)

An expectation is a probability-weighted average over repeated runs, not a lower bound on an individual outcome. Fewer successes still have positive probability.
questions.hint_html: Do not confuse a condition on the expected count with a condition on the probability of reaching that count.

questions.title: A ratio of neighbouring probabilities
questions.prompt_html:
The random variable \(X\) has distribution \(\mathrm B(n,p)\), where \(0<p<1\). It is given that \(\mathrm E(X)=6\) and \(\mathrm P(X=1)=\frac{48}{5}\mathrm P(X=0)\).

  1. Find \(p\) and \(n\).

    Give your answers in exact form.

    [5]

  2. Find \(\mathrm P(X\geq2)\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write each of the two probabilities in full before cancelling their common factors.

\[\frac{\mathrm P(X=1)}{\mathrm P(X=0)}=\frac{np(1-p)^{n-1}}{(1-p)^n}=\frac{np}{1-p}.\]\[\frac{6}{1-p}=\frac{48}{5},\quad 1-p=\frac{5}{8},\quad p=\frac{3}{8},\quad n=16.\]

(b)

\[1-\mathrm P(X=0)-\mathrm P(X=1)=1-\left(\frac{5}{8}\right)^{16}-\binom{16}{1}\left(\frac{3}{8}\right)^{1}\left(\frac{5}{8}\right)^{15}=0.994.\]
questions.hint_html: Dividing P(X=1) by P(X=0) removes most of the powers. Use the mean to eliminate np.

marking_criteria.description_html: Correct complement using the recovered parameters.

questions.title: Choosing between two possible probabilities
questions.prompt_html:
The random variable \(X\) has distribution \(\mathrm B(12,p)\). Its variance is \(\frac{9}{4}\). It is also known that \(\mathrm P(X=0)<\mathrm P(X=12)\).

  1. Find both possible values of \(p\) from the variance alone.

    Give your answers in exact form.

    [3]

  2. Use the additional information to determine \(p\).

    Give your answer in exact form.

    [2]

  3. Find the probability that \(X\) is at least 10.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[12p(1-p)=\frac{9}{4},\quad p^2-p+\frac{3}{16}=0.\]\[(p-\frac{1}{4})(p-\frac{3}{4})=0,\quad p=\frac{1}{4}\text{ or }\frac{3}{4}.\]

(b)

\[(1-p)^{12}<p^{12}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 1-p<p\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p>\frac12.\]

Both bases are positive, so taking the 12th root preserves the inequality. Hence \(p=\frac{3}{4}\).

(c)

\[\mathrm P(10\leq X\leq 12)=\sum_{r=10}^{12}\binom{12}{r}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^r\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{12-r}=0.391\quad\text{(3 s.f.)}.\]
questions.hint_html: The variance cannot distinguish p from 1−p. The endpoint-probability comparison resolves this ambiguity.

marking_criteria.description_html: Forms a quadratic from the variance.
Solves the quadratic retaining both roots.
Uses the comparison of the endpoint probabilities to show p>1/2.
Selects the larger root with justification.

The random variable \(X\) has distribution \(\mathrm B(16,p)\). Its variance is \(\frac{15}{4}\). It is also known that \(\mathrm P(X=0)<\mathrm P(X=16)\).

questions.title: A randomly chosen run length
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Conditional probability (syllabus 5.3).

At the start of a run, a controller chooses \(N=3\) with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\) and \(N=5\) otherwise. It then makes \(N\) independent attempts, each successful with probability \(\frac{3}{5}\). The choice of \(N\) is independent of the attempt outcomes. Let \(X\) be the number of successes.

  1. Find the probability that every attempt in the run succeeds.

    [3]

  2. Given that every attempt succeeded, find the probability that the run contained 5 attempts.

    [3]

  3. Find the expected number of successes per run.

    Give your answer in exact form.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The two run lengths are mutually exclusive possibilities. Average the conditional probabilities, not the number of trials in an exponent.

\[\mathrm P(X=N)=\frac{2}{5}\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^{3}+\frac{3}{5}\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^{5}=0.133.\]

(b)

\[\mathrm P(N=5\mid X=N)=\frac{\frac{3}{5}(\frac{3}{5})^{5}}{\frac{2}{5}(\frac{3}{5})^{3}+\frac{3}{5}(\frac{3}{5})^{5}}=0.351.\]

(c)

For length 3, the mean is \(\frac{9}{5}\); for length 5, it is \(3\). Weight these by the two run-length probabilities.

\[\mathrm E(X)=\frac{2}{5}(\frac{9}{5})+\frac{3}{5}(3)=\frac{63}{25}.\]

questions.title: Locating successes within a run
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Conditional probability (syllabus 5.3); Combinations (syllabus 5.2).

A run contains 12 independent trials, each successful with probability \(\frac{3}{10}\).

  1. Find the probability of exactly 4 successes.

    [2]

  2. Given that there were exactly 4 successes, find the probability that exactly 2 occurred among the first 5 trials.

    [4]

  3. Given the same total of 4 successes, find the probability that the last trial was successful.

    Give your answer in exact form.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\frac{3}{10}\) and \(q_0=1-p=\frac{7}{10}\).

\[\mathrm P(X=4)=\binom{12}{4}\left(\frac{3}{10}\right)^{4}\left(\frac{7}{10}\right)^{8}=0.231\quad\text{(3 s.f.)}.\]

(b)

The numerator requires 2 successes in the first 5 positions and 2 in the remaining 7. On dividing by the probability of 4 successes in the whole run, all factors involving p cancel.

\[\frac{\binom{5}{2}\binom{7}{2}p^{4}(1-p)^{8}}{\binom{12}{4}p^{4}(1-p)^{8}}=\frac{14}{33}=0.424.\]

(c)

All sets of \(4\) successful positions are equally likely under the condition. A specified position belongs to a fraction \(\frac{4}{12}\) of those sets.

\[\frac{\binom{11}{3}}{\binom{12}{4}}=\frac{1}{3}.\]

questions.title: When the source is chosen matters
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Conditional probability (syllabus 5.3).

A record is marked with probability \(\frac{1}{10}\) when produced by source A and \(\frac{2}{5}\) when produced by source B. Conditional on the selected source or sources, record outcomes are independent. A source selection chooses A with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\) and B otherwise.

  1. In procedure I, the source is independently reselected before each of 5 records. Find the probability that none of the records is marked.

    [3]

  2. In procedure II, one source is chosen and used for all 5 records. Find the probability that none is marked.

    [3]

  3. Explain why the same binomial model cannot be used for both procedures.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(0.193\) (3 s.f.).

(b)

\(0.283\) (3 s.f.).

(c)

Procedure II shares a random source, so unconditional independence fails; procedure I reselects independently.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[p=\frac{2}{5}(\frac{1}{10})+\frac{3}{5}(\frac{2}{5})=\frac{7}{25}.\]

The repeated independent source selections give independent outcomes with this common marginal probability.

\[\mathrm P(\text{none})=(1-p)^{5}=0.193.\]

(b)

Condition on the single source selected for the entire run.

\[\frac{2}{5}(\frac{9}{10})^{5}+\frac{3}{5}(\frac{3}{5})^{5}=0.283.\]

(c)

In procedure II the records share an unobserved source. Outcomes are independent conditional on that source, but not unconditionally: seeing one marked record changes the probability that the chosen source was B. Procedure I reselects the source independently each time.
questions.hint_html: For procedure II, choose the source first and then calculate the probability for all the records.

marking_criteria.description_html: Distinguishes independence conditional on a fixed source from unconditional independence.
Explains why fresh independent source selection in procedure I removes that shared-source dependence.

questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Conditional probability (syllabus 5.3).

A record is marked with probability \(\frac{3}{20}\) when produced by source A and \(\frac{7}{20}\) when produced by source B. Conditional on the selected source or sources, record outcomes are independent. A source selection chooses A with probability \(\frac{3}{5}\) and B otherwise.

    [3]

Condition on the single source selected for the entire run.

(c)

In procedure II the records share an unobserved source. Outcomes are independent conditional on that source, but not unconditionally: seeing one marked record changes the probability that the chosen source was B. Procedure I reselects the source independently each time.

questions.title: Three mutually exclusive outcomes
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Conditional probability (syllabus 5.3); Combinations (syllabus 5.2).

An independent request is classified as urgent, routine or deferred with probabilities \(\frac{1}{5}\), \(\frac{3}{10}\) and \(\frac{1}{2}\), respectively. There are 7 requests.

  1. Find the probability that exactly 2 are urgent, 3 are routine and 2 are deferred.

    [4]

  2. Given that none was deferred, find the probability that exactly 2 were urgent.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Choose the urgent positions first, then the routine positions from those remaining. The deferred positions are then fixed.

\[\binom{7}{2}\binom{5}{3}(\frac{1}{5})^{2}(\frac{3}{10})^{3}(\frac{1}{2})^{2}=0.0567.\]

(b)

Conditional on no deferred request, each request is urgent with probability \(\frac{\frac{1}{5}}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{2}{5}\).

\[\mathrm P(X=2)=\binom{7}{2}\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^{5}=0.261\quad\text{(3 s.f.)}.\]
questions.hint_html: The three categories are mutually exclusive. In part (b), change the probability within the restricted population.

marking_criteria.description_html: Chooses positions for the first category.
Chooses positions for the second category from the remainder.
Multiplies by the correct powers of the three probabilities.
Adjusts the individual probability within the two remaining categories.

questions.title: Waiting for an acceptable batch
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: First-success geometric models in this chapter.

A batch contains 10 independent readings, each with the same probability of a fault. The mean number of faults per batch is \(\frac{6}{5}\). A batch is acceptable if it contains at most one fault. Successive batches are independent.

  1. Find the fault probability for one reading and the probability that a batch is acceptable.

    Give the fault probability in exact form and the acceptable-batch probability to 3 significant figures.

    [4]

  2. Find the probability that the first acceptable batch is batch 4.

    [2]

  3. Find the expected number of batches inspected up to and including the first acceptable batch.

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[p=\frac{6}{5}/10=\frac{3}{25}.\]\[q=\mathrm P(X\leq1)=(\frac{22}{25})^{10}+\binom{10}{1}\left(\frac{3}{25}\right)^{1}\left(\frac{22}{25}\right)^{9}=0.658.\]

(b)

Now a trial is a whole batch. The preceding batches must all be unacceptable.

\[(1-q)^{3}q=0.0263.\]

(c)

\[T\sim\operatorname{Geo}(q),\quad \mathrm E(T)=\frac1q=1.52.\]
questions.hint_html: There are two different meanings of success: a faulty reading and an acceptable batch.

questions.prompt_html:
The number \(X\) of completed tasks in a session has distribution \(\mathrm B(12,\frac{11}{20})\). You may assume that its most likely value is one of 6 and 7. Different sessions are independent.

    [3]

  3. Find the probability that each of the next two sessions has this most likely count.

    [2]

(a)

\[\mathrm E(X)=12(\frac{11}{20})=\frac{33}{5}.\]

(b)

\[\mathrm P(X=6)=0.212,\qquad \mathrm P(X=7)=0.222.\]

Comparison using the unrounded values shows that \(7\) is the more likely count. Rounding the mean is not a general way to find a mode.

(c)

\[[\mathrm P(X=7)]^2=0.0495.\]

questions.title: The most likely count
questions.prompt_html:
The number \(X\) of completed tasks in a session has distribution \(\mathrm B(15,\frac{7}{20})\). You may assume that its most likely value is one of 5 and 6. Different sessions are independent.

  1. Find \(\mathrm E(X)\).

    Give your answer in exact form.

    [1]

  2. Determine the most likely value of \(X\), showing your comparison.

    [3]

  3. Find the probability that each of the next two sessions has this most likely count.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\mathrm E(X)=15(\frac{7}{20})=\frac{21}{4}.\]

(b)

\[\mathrm P(X=5)=0.212,\qquad \mathrm P(X=6)=0.191.\]

Comparison using the unrounded values shows that \(5\) is the more likely count. Rounding the mean is not a general way to find a mode.

(c)

\[[\mathrm P(X=5)]^2=0.0451.\]
questions.hint_html: Compare the two probabilities directly. Do not assume that rounding the mean gives the most likely outcome.

questions.title: Equal means do not determine the distribution
questions.prompt_html:
Plan A uses 12 independent attempts, each with success probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). Plan B uses 6 independent attempts, each with success probability \(\frac{1}{2}\). Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be their respective success counts.

  1. Find the mean and variance of each count.

    Give your answers in exact form.

    [4]

  2. Determine which plan gives a larger probability of at least one success. Justify your answer.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(\mathrm E(X)=3\); \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{9}{4}\); \(\mathrm E(Y)=3\); \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\frac{3}{2}\).

(b)

\(\mathrm P(\text{A})=0.968\); \(\mathrm P(\text{B})=0.984\) (3 s.f.).

Plan B.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\mathrm E(X)=3,\quad\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{9}{4}.\]\[\mathrm E(Y)=3,\quad\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\frac{3}{2}.\]

(b)

\[\mathrm P(X\geq1)=1-(\frac{3}{4})^{12}=0.968.\]\[\mathrm P(Y\geq1)=1-(\frac{1}{2})^{6}=0.984.\]

Plan B has the larger probability. The equal means do not imply equal probabilities for individual events.
questions.hint_html: Calculate each probability separately; knowing the common mean is not enough.

marking_criteria.description_html: Uses a complement for each plan.
Correctly identifies plan B using the comparison.

questions.title: Waiting for a valid signal
questions.prompt_html:
A receiver tests independent signals. Each signal is valid with probability \(\frac{11}{50}\). The random variable \(T\) is the number of signals tested up to and including the first valid signal.

  1. Find \(\mathrm P(T=6)\).

    [2]

  2. Find \(\mathrm P(T<8)\).

    [2]

  3. Find \(\mathrm E(T)\).

    Give your answer in exact form.

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\frac{11}{50}\) and \(q_0=1-p=\frac{39}{50}\).

The first 5 trials must fail, followed by a success on trial 6.

\[\mathrm P(T=6)=\left(\frac{39}{50}\right)^{5}\left(\frac{11}{50}\right)=0.0635.\]

(b)

Fewer than 8 signals means success among the first 7.

\[1-(\frac{39}{50})^{7}=0.824.\]

(c)

\[T\sim\operatorname{Geo}(\frac{11}{50}),\quad \mathrm E(T)=\frac1p=\frac{50}{11}.\]
questions.hint_html: The successful signal is included in T. Translate “fewer than” into an integer bound before using a complement.

marking_criteria.description_html: Uses r−1 failures followed by a success.
Uses the complement with the correct strict-bound exponent.
Correct geometric expectation including the successful trial.

questions.title: A paired test
questions.prompt_html:
A paired test uses two independent indicators. The first is green with probability \(\frac{3}{5}\) and the second with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). A paired test is successful only if both indicators are green. All paired tests are independent. Let \(T\) be the number of paired tests up to and including the first success.

  1. Find the success probability for one paired test and \(\mathrm E(T)\).

    Give your answers in exact form.

    [2]

  2. Find the probability that the first successful paired test is test 6 or test 7.

    [3]

  3. Find the probability of requiring more than 8 paired tests.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[p=\frac{3}{5}\times\frac{2}{5}=\frac{6}{25},\quad \mathrm E(T)=\frac1p=\frac{25}{6}.\]

(b)

The two possible first-success times are disjoint.

\[(\frac{19}{25})^{5}(\frac{6}{25})+(\frac{19}{25})^{6}(\frac{6}{25})=0.107.\]

(c)

This requires all of the first 8 paired tests to fail.

\[\mathrm P(T>8)=(\frac{19}{25})^{8}=0.111.\]
questions.hint_html: First calculate the probability that one complete paired test succeeds.

questions.title: A deadline for the first success
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Conditional probability (syllabus 5.3).

A system makes independent attempts, each successful with probability \(\frac{17}{100}\). It stops immediately at the first success. Let \(T\) be the number of attempts performed.

  1. Find the least integer \(N\) for which \(\mathrm P(T\leq N)>\frac{19}{20}\).

    [3]

  2. For this value of \(N\), find the probability that success occurs on attempt \(N\), given that it occurs by attempt \(N\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\frac{17}{100}\) and \(q_0=1-p=\frac{83}{100}\).

\[1-(\frac{83}{100})^N>\frac{19}{20},\quad N>\frac{\ln(\frac{1}{20})}{\ln(\frac{83}{100})}=16.077599.\]

For N=16, the cumulative probability is 0.9492718; for N=17, it is 0.9578956. Hence the least integer is 17.

(b)

\[\mathrm P(T=N\mid T\leq N)=\frac{(1-p)^{N-1}p}{1-(1-p)^N}=0.00900.\]
questions.hint_html: The integer threshold must satisfy a strict inequality. Conditioning on success by the deadline requires division by that event.

Correct least integer and boundary check.
Uses first success exactly at N in the numerator.
Divides by the probability of success by N.

questions.title: Continuing after several failures
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Conditional probability (syllabus 5.3).

Independent attempts succeed with probability \(\frac{1}{5}\). Let \(T\) count attempts including the first success. It is known that the first 5 attempts have all failed.

  1. Find the probability that success occurs in the next 4 attempts.

    [3]

  2. Find the expected number of additional attempts, including the successful one. Justify the distribution you use.

    Give your answer in exact form.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\frac{1}{5}\) and \(q=1-p=\frac{4}{5}\).

Use conditional probability; the conditioning event has probability \(q^{5}\), where \(q=1-p\).

\[\mathrm P(T\leq 9\mid T>5)=\frac{q^{5}-q^{9}}{q^{5}}=1-q^{4}=0.590.\]

(b)

For any positive integer \(j\),

\[\mathrm P(T-5=j\mid T>5)=\frac{q^{5+j-1}p}{q^{5}}=q^{j-1}p.\]

Thus the additional waiting time has the same geometric distribution; no memorised memoryless formula is needed.

\[\mathrm E(\text{additional attempts})=\frac1p=5.\]
questions.hint_html: The failed attempts are already known; do not include their probability again in the final conditional result.

questions.title: Continuing after several failures
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Conditional probability (syllabus 5.3).

Independent attempts succeed with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). Let \(T\) count attempts including the first success. It is known that the first 6 attempts have all failed.

  1. Find the probability that success occurs in the next 5 attempts.

    Give your answer in exact form.

questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\frac{1}{4}\) and \(q=1-p=\frac{3}{4}\).

Use conditional probability; the conditioning event has probability \(q^{6}\), where \(q=1-p\).

\[\mathrm P(T\leq 11\mid T>6)=\frac{q^{6}-q^{11}}{q^{6}}=1-q^{5}=0.763.\]

(b)

For any positive integer \(j\),

\[\mathrm P(T-6=j\mid T>6)=\frac{q^{6+j-1}p}{q^{6}}=q^{j-1}p.\]

Thus the additional waiting time has the same geometric distribution; no memorised memoryless formula is needed.

\[\mathrm E(\text{additional attempts})=\frac1p=4.\]

questions.title: A capped search
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Finite probability tables and moments (syllabus 5.4); Conditional probability (syllabus 5.3).

Each independent test succeeds with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). Testing stops at the first success or after 4 tests, whichever occurs first. Let \(T\) be the number of tests actually performed.

  1. Draw up the probability distribution table for \(T\).

    Give the probabilities as exact fractions.

    [4]

  2. Find \(\mathrm E(T)\).

    [2]

  3. Given that 4 tests were performed, find the probability that the final test succeeded.

    Give your answer in exact form.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\frac{1}{4}\) and \(q=1-p=\frac{3}{4}\).

For t<4, stopping requires a success at t. Reaching test 4 requires only 3 failures: both outcomes of the final test stop the procedure.

\[\mathrm P(T=4)=q^{3}p+q^{4}=q^{3}.\]
\(T\)\(\mathrm P(T=t)\)
\(1\)\(\frac{1}{4}\)
\(2\)\(\frac{3}{16}\)
\(3\)\(\frac{9}{64}\)
\(4\)\(\frac{27}{64}\)

(b)

\[\mathrm E(T)=\sum_{t=1}^{4}t\mathrm P(T=t)=\frac{175}{64}=2.73.\]

(c)

\[\frac{q^{3}p}{q^{3}}=p=\frac{1}{4}.\]

questions.title: A change of procedure
questions.prompt_html:
A sequence of independent tests is performed. Each of the first 4 tests has success probability \(\frac{1}{6}\). Each subsequent test has success probability \(\frac{1}{3}\). Testing stops at the first success, and \(T\) is the number of tests performed.

  1. Explain why \(T\) does not have a geometric distribution with one constant parameter.

    [1]

  2. Find the probability that the first success is on test 6.

    [3]

  3. Find the probability that the first success is by test 9.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

The success probability is not constant across all trials.

(b)

\(0.107\) (3 s.f.).

(c)

\(0.936\) (3 s.f.).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The success probability changes after the 4th test. A single geometric distribution requires a constant success probability at every trial.

(b)

The first 4 tests fail under the original procedure; a further 1 tests fail under the new procedure before its first success.

\[(\frac{5}{6})^{4}(\frac{2}{3})^{1}(\frac{1}{3})=0.107.\]

(c)

The complement consists of failure of every test up to the deadline, with the two probabilities used over their correct time periods.

\[1-(\frac{5}{6})^{4}(\frac{2}{3})^{5}=0.936.\]

questions.title: Recovering a geometric parameter from tails
questions.prompt_html:
The random variable \(T\) has a geometric distribution with unknown success probability \(p\), where \(0<p<1\). It is given that \(\mathrm P(T>5)=\frac{16}{25}\mathrm P(T>3)\).

  1. Find \(p\).

    Give your answer in exact form.

    [3]

  2. In a new run of exactly 10 independent trials with this success probability, find the probability of at least 3 successes.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[(1-p)^{5}=\frac{16}{25}(1-p)^{3}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (1-p)^2=\frac{16}{25}.\]

The factor cancelled is non-zero. Since \(0<1-p<1\), take the positive root.

\[1-p=\frac{4}{5},\quad p=\frac{1}{5}.\]

(b)

The new variable counts successes in a fixed number of trials, so it is binomial, not geometric.

\[\mathrm P(3\leq X\leq 10)=\sum_{r=3}^{10}\binom{10}{r}\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^r\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)^{10-r}=0.322\quad\text{(3 s.f.)}.\]
questions.hint_html: Divide the tail probabilities first. The second part counts successes rather than waiting for the first one.

marking_criteria.description_html: Expresses both tail probabilities using powers of 1−p.
Cancels and selects the admissible root.

questions.title: The second successful attempt
questions.prompt_html:
Attempts are independent and each succeeds with probability \(\frac{7}{25}\). Testing continues after a success.

  1. Find the probability that the second success is on attempt 7.

    [3]

  2. Find the probability that the second success occurs before attempt 10.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\frac{7}{25}\) and \(q_0=1-p=\frac{18}{25}\).

Exactly one of the first 6 attempts must succeed, and attempt 7 must succeed. The earlier success has 6 possible positions.

\[\binom{6}{1}p(1-p)^{5}p=6(\frac{7}{25})^2(\frac{18}{25})^{5}=0.0910.\]

(b)

This is the event of at least two successes in the first 9 attempts, not first success before the bound.

\[1-\mathrm P(\mathrm B(9,\frac{7}{25})=0)-\mathrm P(\mathrm B(9,\frac{7}{25})=1)=0.766.\]

questions.title: A first-success condition and a second-success deadline
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Conditional probability (syllabus 5.3).

Independent attempts succeed with probability \(\frac{13}{50}\). Testing continues after each success.

  1. Find the probability that the second success occurs before attempt 8.

    [3]

  2. Given that the first success occurred on or before attempt 3, find the probability that the second success occurs before attempt 8.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\frac{13}{50}\) and \(q=1-p=\frac{37}{50}\).

This is at least two successes in 7 attempts.

\[1-\sum_{r=0}^{1}\binom{7}{r}\left(\frac{13}{50}\right)^r\left(\frac{37}{50}\right)^{7-r}=0.580.\]

(b)

Let A be the second-success deadline event and B the first-success condition. Remove from A those histories with no success in the first 3 attempts.

\[\mathrm P(A\cap B)=\mathrm P(A)-q^{3}\mathrm P(\mathrm B(4,p)\geq2).\]\[\mathrm P(A\mid B)=\frac{\mathrm P(A)-q^{3}[1-\sum_{r=0}^{1}\binom{4}{r}\left(\frac{13}{50}\right)^r\left(\frac{37}{50}\right)^{4-r}]}{1-q^{3}}=0.785.\]

The first-success condition does not specify the exact first-success time, so it cannot be replaced by a fixed starting time.

questions.prompt_html:

questions.prompt_html:

questions.prompt_html:
A round contains four independent checks, each successful with probability \(\frac{1}{3}\). A round qualifies if at least three checks succeed. Rounds are independent and continue after qualifying rounds.

(c)

For each specified last round, choose the one earlier qualifying round. Add the two disjoint final-round events.

\[(6)q^2(1-q)^{5}+7q^2(1-q)^{6}=0.0837.\]

questions.prompt_html:
A round contains four independent checks, each successful with probability \(\frac{3}{5}\). A round qualifies if at least three checks succeed. Rounds are independent and continue after qualifying rounds.

  1. Find the probability that one round qualifies.

    [3]

  2. Find the probability that the first qualifying round is round 5.

    [2]

  3. Find the probability that the second qualifying round is round 7 or round 8.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[q=\binom{4}{3}(\frac{3}{5})^3(\frac{2}{5})+(\frac{3}{5})^4=\frac{297}{625}.\]

(b)

A trial is now a complete round.

\[(1-q)^{4}q=0.0360.\]

(c)

For each specified last round, choose the one earlier qualifying round. Add the two disjoint final-round events.

\[(6)q^2(1-q)^{5}+7q^2(1-q)^{6}=0.0870.\]

questions.title: With and without returning a record
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Finite probability tables and moments (syllabus 5.4).

A directory contains 3 usable records and 4 expired records. Every selection is uniformly random among the records currently available. Two separate procedures begin with the full directory.

  1. In procedure I, each selected record is returned before the next selection. Find the probability that the first usable record is found on selection 3.

    [2]

  2. In procedure II, selected records are not returned. Let \(T\) be the number of selections up to and including the first usable record. Draw up the distribution table of \(T\).

    Give the probabilities as exact fractions.

    [4]

  3. For procedure II, find \(\mathrm E(T)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(T)\).

    Give your answers in exact form.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Returning the record keeps the success probability constant at \(\frac{3}{7}\).

The first 2 trials must fail, followed by a success on trial 3.

(b)

Multiply the changing conditional probabilities. For example, \(\mathrm P(T=2)=\frac{4}{7}\frac{3}{6}\). No more than 5 selections are possible before a usable record appears.

\(T\)\(\mathrm P(T=t)\)

\(2\)\(\frac{2}{7}\)
\(3\)\(\frac{6}{35}\)
\(4\)\(\frac{3}{35}\)

\[\mathrm E(T)=\sum t\mathrm P(T=t)=2,\quad \mathrm E(T^2)=\sum t^2\mathrm P(T=t)=\frac{26}{5}.\]\[\operatorname{Var}(T)=\mathrm E(T^2)-[\mathrm E(T)]^2=\frac{6}{5}.\]

questions.title: From an incomplete score distribution to repeated trials
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Finite probability tables and moments (syllabus 5.4).

Each independent reading has score \(S\) with the following distribution. The mean score is \(\frac{33}{20}\).

\(\mathrm P(S=s)\)\(\frac{1}{4}\)\(u\)\(v\)\(\frac{1}{10}\)

  1. Find \(u\) and \(v\).

    Give your answers in exact form.

    [4]

  2. Find the probability that at least 3 of 8 readings have score 3.

    [3]

  3. Find the probability that score 3 first appears on reading 5.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[u+v=\frac{13}{20},\quad u+3v+4(\frac{1}{10})=\frac{33}{20}.\]\[2v=\frac{3}{5},\quad v=\frac{3}{10},\quad u=\frac{7}{20}.\]

(b)

A success is a score of 3, which has probability v.

\[\mathrm P(3\leq X\leq 8)=\sum_{r=3}^{8}\binom{8}{r}\left(\frac{3}{10}\right)^r\left(\frac{7}{10}\right)^{8-r}=0.448\quad\text{(3 s.f.)}.\]

(c)

The first 4 trials must fail, followed by a success on trial 5.

\[\mathrm P(T=5)=\left(\frac{7}{10}\right)^{4}\left(\frac{3}{10}\right)=0.0720.\]

questions.title: Sessions selected by a deadline
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Conditional probability (syllabus 5.3); Finite probability tables and moments (syllabus 5.4).

In each independent session, tests are performed until the first success. Each test succeeds independently with probability \(\frac{6}{25}\). Let \(T\) be the number of tests up to and including the first success. A session is described as prompt if \(T\leq 6\).

  1. Find the probability that a session is prompt.

    [2]

  2. A prompt session is selected. Find the probability that its first success was on test 4.

    [2]

  3. Find the probability that exactly 3 of 5 new sessions are prompt.

    [3]

  4. Find the expected number of tests in a prompt session.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\frac{6}{25}\) and \(q_0=1-p=\frac{19}{25}\).

\[q=\mathrm P(T\leq 6)=1-(\frac{19}{25})^{6}=0.807.\]

(b)

\[\mathrm P(T=4\mid T\leq 6)=\frac{(\frac{19}{25})^{3}(\frac{6}{25})}{1-(\frac{19}{25})^{6}}=0.131.\]

(c)

\[\binom{5}{3}q^{3}(1-q)^{2}=0.195.\]

Here q denotes the unrounded prompt-session probability from part (a), not the failure probability of one test.

(d)

The geometric mean 1/p refers to all sessions, not the selected prompt sessions. Use the conditional finite probabilities.

\[\mathrm E(T\mid T\leq 6)=\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{6}t(1-p)^{t-1}p}{1-(1-p)^{6}}=\frac{29941823}{10949708}=2.73.\]

questions.title: Sessions selected by a deadline
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Conditional probability (syllabus 5.3); Finite probability tables and moments (syllabus 5.4).

In each independent session, tests are performed until the first success. Each test succeeds independently with probability \(\frac{9}{50}\). Let \(T\) be the number of tests up to and including the first success. A session is described as prompt if \(T\leq 5\).

  1. Find the probability that a session is prompt.

    [2]

  2. A prompt session is selected. Find the probability that its first success was on test 3.

    [2]

  3. Find the probability that exactly 2 of 5 new sessions are prompt.

    [3]

  4. Find the expected number of tests in a prompt session.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\frac{9}{50}\) and \(q_0=1-p=\frac{41}{50}\).

\[q=\mathrm P(T\leq 5)=1-(\frac{41}{50})^{5}=0.629.\]

(b)

\[\mathrm P(T=3\mid T\leq 5)=\frac{(\frac{41}{50})^{2}(\frac{9}{50})}{1-(\frac{41}{50})^{5}}=0.192.\]

(c)

\[\binom{5}{2}q^{2}(1-q)^{3}=0.202.\]

Here q denotes the unrounded prompt-session probability from part (a), not the failure probability of one test.

(d)

The geometric mean 1/p refers to all sessions, not the selected prompt sessions. Use the conditional finite probabilities.

\[\mathrm E(T\mid T\leq 5)=\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{5}t(1-p)^{t-1}p}{1-(1-p)^{5}}=\frac{57020505}{21849311}=2.61.\]

questions.title: Stopping at a decision
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Conditional probability (syllabus 5.3); Finite probability tables and moments (syllabus 5.4).

A component is checked repeatedly. Each independent check is passed with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\). Checking stops immediately when either three passes or two failures have occurred. The component is accepted if three passes occur first. Let \(T\) be the number of checks performed.

  1. Find the probability that the component is accepted.

    [3]

  2. Draw up the probability distribution table for \(T\).

    Give the probabilities as exact fractions.

    [4]

  3. Given that four checks were needed, find the probability that the component was accepted.

    Give your answer in exact form.

    [2]

  4. Find \(\mathrm E(T)\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(p=\frac{2}{5}\) and \(q=1-p=\frac{3}{5}\).

Acceptance at check 3 requires PPP. Acceptance at check 4 requires exactly two passes in the first three checks and a pass on check 4. These earlier three checks cannot already contain two failures.

\[\mathrm P(\text{accepted})=p^3+\binom{3}{1}p^3(1-p)=\frac{112}{625}=0.179.\]

(b)

Stopping at 2 occurs only for FF. Stopping at 3 occurs for PPP, PFF or FPF. To reach check 4, the first three checks contain exactly two passes and one failure; either outcome at check 4 then stops the procedure.

\[\mathrm P(T=2)=q^2,\quad \mathrm P(T=3)=p^3+2pq^2,\quad \mathrm P(T=4)=3p^2q.\]
\(T\)\(\mathrm P(T=t)\)
\(2\)\(\frac{9}{25}\)
\(3\)\(\frac{44}{125}\)
\(4\)\(\frac{36}{125}\)

(c)

\[\mathrm P(\text{accepted}\mid T=4)=\frac{3p^3q}{3p^2q}=p.\]

Equivalently, every history reaching check 4 has two passes and one failure, so acceptance is determined by the final independent check.

(d)

\[\mathrm E(T)=2q^2+3(p^3+2pq^2)+4(3p^2q)=\frac{366}{125}=2.93.\]
